model.transport: fresh isolated tool-enabled agent; tools only read prompts and serialize explicit judgments
model.blinding: procedural file-access restrictions, not an operating-system access guarantee

rows.text:
New members get a picture guide to the studio and walk through it at their own pace. Ask them to talk the steward through a session afterward so there is time to clear up any gaps before they start working on their own. For each round of bookings, the steward puts up a list showing whose turn it is to choose from the session sheet. Give different people the first picks from round to round. Each member chooses among the remaining bench times to suit their schedule. A person who turns up can use a session nobody has taken.

Try the material on a small working sample before planning the rest of the project. With the results in hand, the member puts the next steps, the supplies to get ready and the intended stopping point on their project card. Tools each have a numbered hook and a matching space for the borrower's name. Sign there before taking the tool, and bring it back during the same session. Someone who comes across an empty hook can see whom to ask. If something feels or looks wrong in use, set the tool aside immediately in the tray for faulty tools. Whoever spotted the fault should describe the experience on a repair card, giving the steward both a tool safely withdrawn from use and particulars for the person inspecting it.

Members can leave a short question under the relevant subject on the help list and get on with any work they can safely manage. The steward can bring people with the same question together for one explanation. A question that crops up repeatedly also makes a good choice for the week's optional demonstration. Invite members to the demonstration corner so those new to the technique have a chance to learn it before they run into difficulty.

Tell the people around the noisy-work station when you are going to hammer and wait for them to respond before you begin. They may need a moment to put delicate work on hold. Anyone leaving a wet piece to dry chooses an empty spot on the rack and labels the piece with their name and the earliest safe handling time. Others can then judge when drying space might become available. To store a project until another visit, pack it, label it with the owner's name and a date for review, and take it to the steward. The steward allocates a vacant shelf space within that member's usual allowance and records where to retrieve the project.

As you produce usable, clean scraps, compare them with the samples beside the labeled bins and drop them into the appropriate one for others to use. For spare material belonging to individual members, the steward collects offers labeled with the amounts and the conditions attached. Bring the owners and prospective takers together once a week so they can discuss an offer before anyone accepts. At the close of each day the studio opens, the steward takes stock of shared supplies and updates the restocking card with the counts and any deliveries already on order. This lets the person ordering consider several shortages at once.

Neighbors should spend the last few minutes of a session checking both their benches together. Finish the cleanup list at one before moving to the other so that both people can look for missed scraps and tools. When members next come in, have them read the dated notices on the board and mark their acknowledgment beside their names before they start. The steward can see who needs an individual update. Schedule a walk around the studio together for the outgoing and incoming stewards during their overlap. Enter unfinished jobs in the handover pad along the way so the incoming steward sees where supplies are running low or repairs are needed and knows what remains to be done.

rows.text:
Greet each guest face to face. The host can ask whether they feel like joining a game now or would prefer a few minutes to get comfortable, then note their name and preference on the welcome sheet. That gives the host a starting point for forming groups and gives anyone who came alone a familiar face. Let guests browse the games and mark the ones that catch their interest. The host can suggest games based on those marks and take requests for anything else in the collection that's available.

Invite people who are happy to teach to announce which games they could start. Interested guests can join them for a closer look, ask what playing would involve and meet the other prospective players. Before they start, the host checks that the game accommodates the group. Guests are free to sit this one out and join a later game. When someone arrives late, a welcome volunteer can introduce them at a table nearing the end of play. If they agree to play the next game together, the volunteer makes a note. While waiting, the guest can try any activity from the waiting basket. They return it when the table calls and take the place already agreed.

Lay the printed rules aid where everyone can consult it while the teacher explains the essentials. Once everyone has heard the explanation, take questions and give each player a trial turn with an unfamiliar action. After the last trial, restore the starting position before anyone makes a choice that counts. Learners who would like tactical advice can choose a willing player as their partner before play begins. They can ask that person again whenever they need help. The partner talks over the options quietly, using only what the players involved can see, and leaves the actual move to the learner.

Work back from closing to leave enough time to put the game away. Each group agrees on a finish time, displays it on a card and asks one of the players to warn the table as it draws near. Agree in advance how to record a position if the group wants to resume an unfinished game. The players also choose points during play for a visible timer to give a signal. They can check the time left at those points without anyone having to watch the clock throughout. When players disagree over a rule, stop play and let two of them spend a short time looking it up while the rest wait. Hear their conclusion and use their interpretation. If the question is still open, use the pair's provisional decision for the evening and check it afterward.

Choose a player at each table to keep an ear on the volume. If a long chat is getting loud, they can invite the people talking to continue in the conversation corner before it gets hard to hear play at the next table. A player wanting a snack or drink can arrange a short time away with the group, use the refreshment area and return for their next action. A player who needs a personal break tells the table aloud. Find a place to stop right away, say what action is due next, keep private information protected and hold off on any move that needs the absent player.

At the end of play, everyone helps sort the components into their labeled bags. Before people leave the table, the teacher checks each bag against the list so the whole group is still on hand to look for anything missing. Put the verified game back in the collection. The following day the host invites brief, optional feedback on the games available, how people found a game to join and anything that got in the way of taking part. Guests have had time to reflect by then. Grouping the answers before arranging another evening helps the host recognize issues shared across tables.

rows.text:
Start with the times the rehearsal room is free. The person handling bookings sends the choir a proposed run of dates and gives singers a chance to flag conflicts while there is still room to move things around. Then book the series. At a consistent interval before each booked rehearsal, send a reminder with a link for singers to say whether they'll be there. Pass a summary to the conductor early enough to plan around the expected turnout in each part.

Tell singers which numbered scores they'll need to bring and circulate the approved digital copies early enough for a read at home. The organizer lays out the matching paper copies for people to collect as they arrive. Ask for volunteers to take turns coming early for setup and remind each person of their particular job, whether it's arranging chairs, laying out folders or getting the conductor's stand ready. Rotating the duties spreads the early starts around.

Before setting the rehearsal order, the conductor asks each section leader which prepared pieces their part would most benefit from singing again. Allow for the different sections' needs and the time booked, then share the order ahead of the session. At the outset, tell the singers which stretch of work will end with the main break. That way the choir knows when it will finish a task and rest together, and anyone needing a brief absence can still step out.

Display the familiar warmup sequence approved by the conductor. A different section leader guides each stage, giving several people a short turn leading the choir through its preparation. With the singers seated, have them sing a short phrase for the conductor to assess the sound in the occupied room. The conductor can then ask singers to move their chairs within their sections, keeping accessible routes clear and making sure the cues will be visible from every new seat.

When the choir struggles with a phrase, the conductor listens to what the singers are doing and picks the single likeliest source of the difficulty. Practice that feature in isolation before singing it in the context of the phrase again. During sectional time the conductor stays with the part needing personal attention. The other leaders work simultaneously in separate corners with their own singers on the bars they've been given. All the parts come back together at the end of the allotted time.

Demonstrate how a common entry or cutoff will be signaled and ask singers to mark the cue in their music so they'll remember to look up. After the parts have sung a passage together, hear from one section at a time about what reached their ears. Take turns asking different sections so the conductor hears from around the room before choosing an adjustment. As the conductor changes a dynamic or the shaping of a phrase, singers pencil it into their scores. Revisit the revised bars aloud before dismissal so singers can catch anything they misunderstood. The organizer then circulates the agreed markings with the piece and bar for each.

Group the materials for home practice by the tricky passage that prompted them. For each passage, the conductor indicates the bars and the recordings available for each part, so someone who remembers struggling in rehearsal can find their own line. Close the session by suggesting two priorities for anyone choosing to practice, and specify the bars in the rehearsal notes. Send absent singers those notes and links to both the revised markings and the recordings. They can update their copies and cover the missed work when it suits them before they return.

They can update their copies and cover the missed work when it suits them before they return.

decision_d76a9f779d9b.text: As the conductor changes a dynamic or the shaping of a phrase, singers pencil it into their scores.
Revisit the revised bars aloud before dismissal so singers can catch anything they misunderstood.
The organizer then circulates the agreed markings with the piece and bar for each.

decision_01db0d9ee017.text: Allow for the different sections' needs and the time booked, then share the order ahead of the session.
At the outset, tell the singers which stretch of work will end with the main break.
That way the choir knows when it will finish a task and rest together, and anyone needing a brief absence can still step out.

decision_6bebf95df8b2.text: At a consistent interval before each booked rehearsal, send a reminder with a link for singers to say whether they'll be there.
Pass a summary to the conductor early enough to plan around the expected turnout in each part.

decision_2a6ca4fef878.text: Tell singers which numbered scores they'll need to bring and circulate the approved digital copies early enough for a read at home.
The organizer lays out the matching paper copies for people to collect as they arrive.

decision_ccff2156987f.text: After the parts have sung a passage together, hear from one section at a time about what reached their ears.
Take turns asking different sections so the conductor hears from around the room before choosing an adjustment.

rows.text:
Before the fair, recruit volunteers on each block to ask neighbors what they might bring. Have them report back by category with approximate quantities for planning table space. Talking at the door includes people who might never fill in a form. Check everything against the published criteria when it actually arrives. Let contributors select an arrival slot on a shared intake sheet, leaving some capacity for unscheduled arrivals in every period. Volunteers can see when to expect a rush. The coordinator uses volunteers' preferred duties and available hours to arrange shifts and circulates the roster in advance so people can prepare and uncovered shifts stand out.

At intake, a contributor stays until a volunteer has compared each item with the condition list. This gives them a chance to clear up a question about damage or an absent part before the volunteer accepts it. For every accepted item the volunteer interviews the contributor and writes up the standard label, recording the item's identifying reference, what it is, any limitations and the accessories that go with it. A volunteer completing the label from the answers helps keep descriptions consistent. Tie or bag the parts of complete sets together before sending them out to the floor, with the description visible. Visitors can still tell what's included while the pieces stay together through the afternoon.

Organize the tables by household room, with signs that direct someone after a saucepan to the kitchen goods or someone outfitting a bedroom to the bedroom goods. Leave the aisles open by storing excess goods on reserve shelves. A runner checks the tables at regular intervals and fills newly open spaces with suitable reserve stock, leaving the table volunteers free to attend to visitors.

As visitors come in, the welcome volunteer brings a few together at a time to explain how to look around, claim something, leave it on hold and collect it. Everyone is welcome to give or take without bringing something in exchange. Let the group begin browsing and use the entrance diagram to answer individual questions. Someone who can't find an item can post a request by the appropriate category sign. If a suitable item turns up, the table volunteer takes the request to a central collection point where visitors can look for a match. A request is no guarantee that the item will appear.

For competing requests, enter each person's request and the time on the sheet. Once the short decision period ends, award the item to the earliest recorded requester. The times are available for people to see how the volunteer decided. Anyone with a claim who wishes to continue looking around can bring their goods to the volunteer managing holds. That volunteer writes down the recipient's name and confirms a pickup time no more than twenty minutes away before putting the goods on a shelf. Both know who has the item and when it must be collected.

To take an item home, present the claim record to the volunteer at the outgoing register. The volunteer confirms the claim, enters the item's identifying reference and gives the recipient a checked slip to show on the way out. Complete those steps before handing over the goods. At that same point anyone can request carrying help without explaining why. When the item is ready, the volunteer assigns the next free helper and cart to take it to the nearby pickup area.

At closing, use each contributor's previously recorded instructions to sort the unclaimed items before letting contributors in to collect them. Arrange the returns for easy retrieval and put the donations together for their scheduled pickup after collection ends. Invite visitors, contributors and volunteers to give feedback in separate, brief conversations if they wish. Ask how it went finding and claiming goods and keeping the fair running. Afterward the organizers compare their notes to see how a procedure worked for people in different roles and which changes might benefit several groups.
